title: Lips
description: Conditions affecting the vermilion, the angles of the mouth, and the perioral skin.

problems.description: Red, sore, cracked skin at the corners of the mouth. Often a gold crust by morning. Worse with drooling, dentures, or anaemia.
problems.etiology:
A combined infection at the corners of the mouth. Three usual organisms: **Staphylococcus aureus, β-haemolytic streptococci, and Candida** [1]. The bugs don't get there on their own — they exploit a moist, macerated angle of the mouth that's been set up by something else.

The two big setups:

- **Local**: trauma, drooling, an ill-fitting denture with reduced occlusal vertical dimension that lets the upper lip fold into the lower [1].
- **Systemic**: iron deficiency and vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia [1]. Iron-deficiency anaemia in particular is a well-recognised cause [2], and angular cheilitis is one of the textbook signs of it [3].

What happens is moisture pools in the fold, the skin macerates, and the bug mix moves in. Without fixing the underlying setup, treatment alone runs out of steam [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll see at the corners:

- Red, cracked, macerated skin — often with a gold crust [1].
- Usually bilateral when the cause is denture or systemic; can be unilateral with local trauma.
- Sore but not severely painful. Often splits when the patient yawns or eats.

Look in the rest of the mouth too — angular cheilitis travels with other candidal and denture problems. Denture stomatitis on the palate, papillary hyperplasia under the upper denture, and a smooth red tongue are commonly there alongside [1].
problems.results:
- **Swab from the commissure**: typically grows the staph–strep–Candida mix [1]; in denture-associated cases it often grows S. aureus, sensitive to fusidic acid [4]. Sensitivities steer the topical choice.
- **FBC and haematinics**: iron, ferritin, B12, folate [1]. Microcytic hypochromic picture points hard at iron deficiency [3].
- **Denture assessment**: occlusal vertical dimension, fit, hygiene, age. An overclosed denture sets up the fold [1].
- **Blood glucose** if there's coexisting candidosis — diabetes predisposes to candida.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that distinguishes angular cheilitis from look-alikes: **it's at the angles of the mouth and almost always has a candidal component.**

Compare to:

- **Cold sore**: vesicles on the vermilion or skin near the lip with a tingling prodrome — not strictly at the angle.
- **Contact dermatitis**: itchy, more diffuse, history of new lipstick / toothpaste / chewing gum.
- **Orofacial granulomatosis**: persistent firm lip swelling and cobblestone buccal mucosa; angular cheilitis can develop on top [5].

The bilateral pattern, the gold crust, and the link to a denture or anaemia are the giveaways.
problems.treatment:
Two arms run in parallel — clear the infection, fix the cause [1].

**Topical antifungal/antibacterial:**

- **Miconazole cream** is first-line — covers all three usual organisms (strep, staph, Candida) [1, 6]. Apply qds [6].
- **If swab shows S. aureus**, fusidic acid cream is appropriate [4].
- **Mupirocin to the anterior nares** if Staph keeps coming back — clears the nasal reservoir [1].
- Treat for at least 10 days **after** the lesion looks resolved. Short courses relapse [1].

**Underlying cause:**

- Replace or rebase the denture if the vertical dimension is wrong [1].
- Correct anaemia — iron, B12, or folate replacement under the GP [1].
- Treat coexisting denture stomatitis: leave dentures out at night, soak in chlorhexidine, miconazole gel to the fitting surface.

**Watch-out**: miconazole interacts with warfarin (raises INR), antidiabetics, antiepileptics, and a few other drug classes [7]. Check the medical history before prescribing.
problems.prognosis:
- Treat both arms (infection + cause) → resolves in 1–2 weeks and stays resolved [1].
- Treat the infection only → comes back. The setup is still there [1].
- Keeps recurring without an obvious local cause → think systemic. Anaemia, diabetes, immunosuppression [2, 3].

**Rule of thumb**: angular cheilitis on a denture wearer is a denture problem until proven otherwise. Recurrent bilateral angular cheilitis without dentures deserves bloods.

citations.quote: A combined staphylococcal, β-haemolytic streptococci, and candidal infection, involving the tissues at the angle of the mouth (Fig. 11.1). Aetiology is multifactorial with local and systemic precipitating factors, e.g. trauma, inadequate vertical dimension of denture, iron deficiency, and vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia. Therefore, FBC and haematinics should be investigated. Clinically, red, cracked, macerated skin at angles of the mouth, often with a gold crust. Rx: miconazole cream, which is active against all three infecting organisms. Rx needs to be prolonged, up to 10 days after resolution of clinical lesion, and carried out in conjunction with elimination of any underlying factors. Mupirocin cream applied to the anterior nares helps eradicate sources of Staphylococcus aureus.

Candidosis (…… Oral candidosis (candidiasis), p. 438) may be precipitated or exacerbated by anaemia, particularly iron deficiency, and angular cheilitis is a well-recognized association. The sore, clinically normal tongue (burning tongue) is sometimes a manifestation or even precursor of anaemia.

These are notoriously unreliable, but may include general fatigue, heart failure, angina on effort, pallor (look at conjunctivae and palmar creases, but unreliable), brittle nails &/or spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), oral discomfort &/or ulceration, glossitis, and classically angular cheilitis.
citations.source: Oxford Handbook · paragraph 7182 (signs of iron-deficiency anaemia)

citations.quote: In this case, a swab was taken from the commissure and surrounding skin. Culture revealed Staphylococcus aureus, which was sensitive to fusidic acid.

Lip swelling affects the majority of patients, with each episode lasting days to weeks. Over time, the lips may become firm and persistently swollen. The perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy or cracked, with some patients developing angular cheilitis.
citations.source: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving · paragraph 7906 (orofacial granulomatosis)

citations.quote: This is a useful drug, particularly in management of angular cheilitis, as it is active against streptococci, staphylococci, and Candida. Miconazole oral gel 24mg/mL is of use in chronic mucocutaneous and chronic hyperplastic candidosis. Dose: 2.5mL qds 20mg/g gel. Apply a pea-sized amount after food qds. Can be applied to dentures also. Miconazole cream is used topically for angular cheilitis.

There are recognized potentially serious interactions between miconazole, fluconazole, and related drugs and antibacterials, anticoagulants, antidiabetics, antiepileptics, antihistamines, anxiolytics, cisapride, ciclosporin, and theophylline. Check what your patient is currently taking.

problems.description: Recurring cluster of tiny blisters on the vermilion or the skin just above it. Burning and tingling before the blisters appear. Heals within 1–2 weeks then comes back.
problems.etiology:
The virus responsible is herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). The reason labialis can keep recurring is that HSV-1 doesn't clear after the primary infection — it travels back along sensory axons to the trigeminal or geniculate ganglion and stays there as a latent infection [1]. A viral latency gene and the cell-mediated immune response keep the balance between latency and reactivation [2].

When the balance tips toward reactivation, the virus travels back down the nerve to the skin or mucosa at the mucocutaneous junction of the lip. The reason antibodies don't prevent recurrences is that for most of its life cycle the virus is intracellular, putting it out of reach of the humoral response [2].

Environmental triggers for reactivation include ultraviolet light, illness, and stress [2]. Trauma — for example, removal of a wisdom tooth — and immunosuppression are also recognised precipitants [3].
problems.presentation:
The patient usually knows it's coming before you can see anything. The prodrome is a burning or tingling sensation at the site, lasting up to 24 hours [3]. Then:

- Small vesicles appear at the vermilion border or the skin immediately above or below it [3].
- Vesicles rupture quickly, leaving shallow painful erosions, which crust over.
- Confined to one branch of the trigeminal nerve — usually recurs on the same patch of lip [3].
- Recurrences are seen in up to 30% of patients who have had a primary HSV infection [3].
problems.results:
Herpes labialis is a clinical diagnosis. Special investigations are rarely needed in primary care.

- If there is doubt, viral swab from the lesion base can confirm HSV by PCR.
- The prodrome + vesiculation + mucocutaneous junction site + previous history of recurrences is the defining pattern [2, 3].
- Labial recurrences are painful and unpleasant but relatively readily treated because there is often a characteristic prodromal sensation of burning or itching and the vesicles are easily seen [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that sets herpes labialis apart:

- **Site**: mucocutaneous junction of the lip — not strictly at the angle (angular cheilitis), not diffusely across the mucosa (primary HSV stomatitis).
- **Prodrome**: burning or tingling reliably precedes the vesicles [3]. Angular cheilitis has no prodrome; mucocele has no pain at all.
- **Recurrence pattern**: same site, same nerve territory, same trigger pattern [3].
- **Erythema multiforme connection**: recurrent HSV is a common trigger for erythema multiforme — a cold sore 1–2 weeks before the onset of lip crusting and oral erosions raises this possibility [5].
problems.treatment:
The goal is to start treatment in the prodrome, before vesicles form — that's when antivirals make the most difference [4].

- **Aciclovir 5% cream**: apply to the site of prodromal or early lesion 4-hourly for 5 days [6].
- **Penciclovir 1% cream**: apply 2-hourly for 4 days — also prescribable for herpes labialis [7].
- Both are most effective in the prodromal or early vesicular stage [3, 6]. Started late, they shorten duration but can't abort the episode.
- **Systemic aciclovir** (400mg PO five times daily for 5 days) [6] should be considered in the immunocompromised or for frequent recurrences [3].
- Sun block on the lips reduces UV-triggered recurrences.
problems.prognosis:
- Each episode is self-limiting, resolving in about 1–2 weeks without treatment.
- Up to 30% of people who acquire HSV go on to have recurrent cold sores [8]; many suffer only occasional lesions, and frequency tends to decrease with age.
- In immunocompromised patients, recurrences can be more severe and more frequent — systemic antivirals are the appropriate response [3].
- There is no cure. Latent infection in the ganglion persists for life [2].

citations.quote: During infection, HSV is transported back along axons of sensory nerves to their nuclei. There, the neurones are infected but do not die, and the virus becomes latent – that is, virus persists but no infectious virions are produced.

A viral latency gene and the cell-mediated immune response contribute to the balance between latency and reactivation. If infection is reactivated, the virus travels down the nerve to cause a localized recurrent infection of the mucosa or skin – a cold sore. Because the virus is intracellular for most of this life cycle, antibodies of the humoral immune response are not effective in preventing recurrences. Environmental triggers for cold sores include ultraviolet light, illness and stress.

These are seen in up to 30% of patients affecting the mucocutaneous junction of the lips (herpes labialis, cold sore) and result from reactivation of the 1° infection which is believed to lie dormant in the dorsal root, and autonomic or cranial nerve ganglia (trigeminal or geniculate). Precipitating factors include trauma, e.g. during removal of 8 and immunosuppression and, less commonly, exposure to sunlight, stress, and febrile illness. Usually recurs on area of distribution supplied by one branch of the trigeminal nerve. Prodromal phase (burning/tingling) over 24h is followed by vesiculation and pain. Lesions may respond to 1% penciclovir or aciclovir 5% cream if used in the prodromal stage. Should consider systemic aciclovir (…… Aciclovir, p. 612) in the immunosuppressed or frequent recurrences.

Labial recurrences are painful and unpleasant but relatively readily treated because there is often a characteristic prodromal sensation of burning or itching and the vesicles are easily seen. Early treatment is, therefore, possible, and antiviral drugs can be very effective. Topical preparations of 5% aciclovir are available without prescription.

If the patient has had recurrent HSV infection, usually in the form of herpes labialis, then the present ulcers could not have been caused by a primary herpetic infection. Recurrent herpetic infection is sometimes a trigger for attacks of erythema multiforme and a cold sore 1–2 weeks before onset would raise this possibility.

Active against herpes simplex and zoster; relatively non-toxic and can be given systemically or topically. Dose: herpes labialis: apply 5% aciclovir cream to site of prodromal or early lesion 4-hourly for 5 days; herpetic stomatitis: 200mg PO (400mg in immunocompromised) five times daily for 5 days; herpes zoster: 800mg PO five times daily for 7 days.
Penciclovir as a 1% cream applied 2-hourly for 4 days is prescribable according to the DPF for herpes labialis.

Between 15 and 30% of individuals who come into contact with the virus develop recurrent infection. It is not clear whether those who suffer a symptomatic primary infection such as gingivostomatitis have an increased risk. Although this percentage seems high, many patients with recurrent herpes infection suffer only very occasional lesions.

problems.description: A smooth, soft, painless fluid-filled lump on the inner surface of the lower lip that appeared after lip-biting or minor trauma. Bluish, translucent. Recurs if not fully removed.
problems.etiology:
The mechanism is simple: a minor salivary duct gets traumatised — most often by a bite — and saliva leaks out of the duct into the surrounding connective tissue. The spilled saliva doesn't drain away; instead it pools and is walled off by compressed connective tissue, forming a pseudocyst [1].

The reason mucoceles mostly appear on the lower lip is anatomy: the minor salivary gland ducts of the lower lip are exposed to biting trauma far more than those on the upper lip [1]. This matters clinically — a similar-looking swelling on the upper lip is much more likely to be a minor salivary gland tumour and should be treated with more suspicion [1, 2].

A minority are true mucous retention cysts rather than extravasation pseudocysts [1], but the clinical distinction rarely changes management.
problems.presentation:
- Smooth, soft, dome-shaped swelling on the inner surface of the lower lip, typically 5–10 mm in diameter.
- Bluish or translucent in colour when superficial; flesh-coloured if it lies deeper in the tissue.
- Painless. The patient often presents because they've noticed the lump or keep biting it.
- History of repeated trauma or biting at the site is common.
- May have burst spontaneously before the appointment, leaving a flat, mildly sore area — and then re-formed.
problems.results:
Mucocele is a clinical diagnosis based on site, appearance, and history.

- **Aspiration**: aspirating a thin, clear-to-slightly-viscous fluid (saliva) confirms the diagnosis and differentiates it from a vascular lesion (which would aspirate blood).
- No imaging is required for a straightforward lower-lip mucocele.
- **Histology** after excision is standard practice and confirms the mucous extravasation pattern — compressed connective tissue wall without a true epithelial lining.
- Any swelling on the **upper lip** warrants biopsy and histology rather than clinical assumption: >50% of upper lip minor salivary gland tumours are malignant [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key distinguishing features:

- **Lower lip, inner surface**: this is the signature site. Upper lip swellings are a red flag for salivary tumour [1, 2].
- **Fluctuant and translucent**: unlike a fibrous epulis or fibroma, which are firm and opaque.
- **Bursts and recurs**: spontaneous rupture followed by re-accumulation is almost pathognomonic of mucocele.
- Unlike a ranula (which is a mucocele of the floor of the mouth arising from the sublingual gland [3]), labial mucoceles are superficial and straightforwardly excised.
problems.treatment:
Excision of the mucocele together with the associated damaged minor salivary gland and duct [1]. The reason the gland must come out with the cyst is that leaving it behind almost guarantees recurrence — the damaged duct continues to leak.

- Performed under local anaesthesia in primary care or a minor surgery setting.
- Send the specimen for histology — confirms diagnosis and excludes an unexpected tumour.
- Marsupialisation alone is not recommended; the recurrence rate is high.
- For an **upper lip** swelling: do not assume mucocele. Refer for specialist assessment — the majority of minor salivary gland tumours at this site are malignant [2].
problems.prognosis:
- Excision with the associated gland: low recurrence rate.
- Excision of the cyst alone without the gland: high likelihood of recurrence.
- Natural history without treatment: some smaller mucoceles rupture and resolve spontaneously but most recur. Repeated biting of a persisting mucocele keeps the cycle going.

citations.quote: These are usually mucous extravasation cysts, where saliva leaks from a traumatized duct and pools, creating a compressed connective tissue capsule. Rarely, they are mucous retention cysts. They mostly affect the lower lip—similar swellings in the upper lip are often minor salivary gland tumours (…… Salivary gland tumours, p. 513). Rx: excision with associated damaged glands and duct.

>50% of tumours are malignant (mostly adenoid cystic) and require extensive surgery and reconstruction similar to floor of mouth cancer. Beware the 'mucocele' of the upper lip—it is almost certainly a tumour.

These are mucoceles of the floor of the mouth, arising from the sublingual gland. They tend to recur if marsupialized. A plunging ranula crosses deep to the mylohyoid and appears as a neck and floor of mouth swelling. Rx: excision of cyst and associated sublingual gland; the submandibular gland may have to be excised if the duct is damaged.

problems.description: Painless, non-healing ulcer or thickened white patch on the lower lip vermilion. History of long-term sun exposure. Present for more than 3 weeks.
problems.conditionName: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lip
problems.etiology:
The main aetiological factor in cancer of the lip is exposure to sunlight — the same mechanism as skin cancer [1]. The risk doubles every 250 miles nearer the equator, which is the clearest statement of the dose-response relationship [1]. Actinic cheilitis — sun damage to the lower lip causing excessive keratin production and increased mitotic activity in the basal layer — is the recognised premalignant precursor [2].

The lower lip is almost exclusively affected because it receives direct ultraviolet radiation; the upper lip is shaded by the philtrum. This origin-specific pattern distinguishes lip SCC from intraoral SCC, which is driven more by tobacco and alcohol [1].

Tobacco, alcohol, and immunosuppression (e.g. renal transplant patients, HIV) increase overall risk, and HPV type 16 and 18 infection is now recognised as an independent risk factor for oropharyngeal SCC [1].
problems.presentation:
The clinical picture the source describes:

- A **painless ulcer** with firm raised edges, an indurated, inflamed, granular base, and fixation to surrounding tissues [3]. Pain is usually a late feature [3].
- May present instead as a swelling, a white patch, an erythro-leucoplakia, or an erythroplakia [3].
- Malignancy should be suspected if any such lesion persists for **more than 3 weeks** [3].
- Lower lip vermilion is the classic site. Patient is typically male, sixth or seventh decade, outdoor worker.
- A cervical lymph node may be the presenting complaint if there is already metastatic spread [3].
problems.results:
- **Biopsy** is mandatory — this is the only way to confirm the diagnosis. Refer immediately via the urgent cancer pathway rather than waiting to see if the lesion resolves.
- Histology: SCC. Characteristically shows invasion of deep tissues with cellular pleomorphism and increased nuclear staining [4].
- Staging uses TNM classification. Prognosis for stage I (T1–N0) is >85% at 5 years; stage IV is around 10% [5]. Nodal involvement alone reduces cure rates by 50% [5].
- Presence or absence of extracapsular spread in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The critical distinction from benign lower lip lesions:

- **Duration >3 weeks**: any ulcer or white patch persisting beyond 3 weeks must be referred for biopsy [3]. This threshold exists because benign traumatic ulcers heal; SCC does not.
- **Induration**: the firm, fixed base and raised edges distinguish it from aphthous ulceration (soft, mobile, heals in 2 weeks) and mucocele (fluctuant, smooth, inner surface).
- **Actinic cheilitis** is the premalignant stage — blurred vermilion border, dry, scaled, white patches on the lower lip after years of UV exposure [2]. The transition from premalignant to malignant is the clinical worry.
- Unlike intraoral SCC where floor of mouth and lateral tongue are the highest-risk sites, lip SCC is dominated by sun exposure rather than tobacco/alcohol.
problems.treatment:
The goal is surgical excision, usually combined with radiotherapy for advanced disease.

- **Immediate urgent referral** via the two-week-wait cancer pathway. Do not wait, do not treat empirically.
- Management decisions are based on TNM stage and the patient's fitness for surgery [6].
- In many instances of oral cancer, combined surgery and radiotherapy constitutes optimal treatment [6].
- Pre-malignant actinic cheilitis: advise sun block and arrange regular follow-up [2]. If active intervention is indicated, laser excision or vermilionectomy are options.
- Stopping smoking is part of the treatment plan for any tobacco-related risk [1].
problems.prognosis:
- Stage I (T1–N0): >85% survival at 5 years [5].
- Stage IV: approximately 10% survival at 5 years [5].
- Nodal involvement reduces cure rates by 50% [5].
- Overall oral cancer mortality rate is just over 50% despite treatment [7]. Oral cancer is preventable in 75% of cases [7].
- Early diagnosis is the single biggest lever — the stage at presentation determines survival more than the treatment modality.

citations.quote: The main aetiological factor in cancer of the lip is exposure to sunlight, as with skin cancer. It is estimated that the risk of developing lip cancer doubles every 250 miles nearer the equator. Excessive alcohol and tobacco use are the important factors in the aetiology of cancer of the mouth showing a 'synergistic effect'. Perhaps the most clear-cut aetiological factor is the chewing of tobacco and paan. HPV type 16 and 18 infection is now recognized as an independent risk factor for oropharyngeal SCC. Immunosuppression, e.g. in renal transplant patients or patients with HIV, ↑ the risk of this and other tumours.
Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and ↑ mitotic activity in the basal layer. Premalignant. Advise sun blocks and regular follow-up.

Oral cancer is most often seen as a painless ulcer, although it may present as a swelling or as an area of leucoplakia, erythroleucoplakia, or erythroplakia. Patients may present with a history of a neck lump as a result of metastatic spread to cervical lymph nodes. Malignancy should be suspected if any of these lesions persists for >3 weeks. Pain is usually a late feature. Referred otalgia is a common manifestation of pain from the tongue or oropharyngeal cancer. The ulcer is described as firm with raised edges, with an indurated, inflamed, granular base and is fixed to surrounding tissues.

Mostly SCC. Characteristically shows invasion of deep tissues with cellular pleomorphism and ↑ nuclear staining. The presence of a lymphocytic response may have prognostic value, as does the manner of invasion (pushing or spreading). Can spread via local infiltration or lymphatic system (cervical nodes), and late spread via bloodstream.

This is dependent on site and stage,3 (prognosis for stage I is >85% and for stage IV is 10% over 5yrs), and co-morbidity. The presence or absence of extracapsular spread of tumour in metastatic cervical nodes is the most important single prognostic factor. Nodal involvement ↓ cure rates by 50%.

Various parameters affect the choice of Rx for patients with oral cancer; not least among these, but often forgotten, are the patients themselves, their general health, understanding of their disease, geographical location, and social and domestic commitments. Classically, broad Rx principles are based on tumour staging, using the Tumour, Node, Metastasis (TNM) classification, and the patient's fitness for surgery. In many instances of oral cancer, combined surgery and radiotherapy constitutes optimal Rx.

Cancer of the mouth (Fig. 11.4) accounts for ~2% of all malignant tumours in northern Europe and the US, but ~30–40% in the Indian subcontinent. >90% of these are SCCs. Globally it is the sixth commonest cause of cancer-related death. >2000 new cases of oral cancer are registered per year in the UK and each year half that number die from or with the disease. Oral cancer is preventable in 75% of cases. Overall mortality rate is just over 50% despite Rx.

problems.description: Dry, peeling, or cracked lips with no specific site. The patient habitually licks or picks at them. No blistering, no commissure involvement.
problems.conditionName: Cheilitis simplex (lip licker's dermatitis / dry sore lips)
problems.etiology:
The most common cause is a habit cycle: the lips feel dry, the patient licks them, the saliva evaporates and leaves them drier than before, so they lick again [1]. Wind exposure and sunlight cause direct drying of the vermilion, which has no sebaceous glands to maintain its moisture barrier. Viral illness can present this way too [1].

The reason the cycle perpetuates is mechanical: repeated wetting and drying of the vermilion disrupts the epithelium's barrier function. Skin around the mouth may show a faint ring of redness tracing the extent of the tongue's reach — the classic "licker's border".

This is distinguished from actinic cheilitis (which is premalignant, driven by UV, and shows keratotic changes) and exfoliative cheilitis (persistent crusting and scaling of unknown aetiology, more severe) by its self-sustaining habit aetiology and its benign, reversible course.
problems.presentation:
- Dry, cracked, peeling vermilion — often worse in winter or during illness.
- Mild soreness but no vesiculation, no ulceration, no gold crusting at the angles.
- In children and younger adults: a visible perioral ring of slight redness or hyperpigmentation tracing the licking habit.
- Patient often aware of the habit; may also report picking or peeling the dry skin.
- No systemic symptoms. No lymphadenopathy.
problems.results:
No investigations are routinely needed. This is a clinical diagnosis based on history and pattern.

- If the appearance is persistent, unusual, or associated with systemic features, consider:
  - **Patch testing** to exclude contact allergic cheilitis from toothpaste, lipstick, or food flavourings.
  - **FBC and haematinics** if there is also angular cheilitis or a burning tongue — haematinic deficiency contributes.
- The absence of vesicles, the absence of commissure involvement, and the licking history distinguish this from herpes labialis and angular cheilitis respectively.
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key framing: **this is a habit-driven condition, not an infective one.**

- No vesicles (unlike herpes labialis), no commissure involvement (unlike angular cheilitis), no persistent crusting (unlike exfoliative cheilitis).
- The perioral ring of redness from licking is specific to this condition when present.
- Responds promptly to barrier treatment and habit interruption — that response itself helps confirm the diagnosis.
- Exfoliative cheilitis is sometimes described as similar to actinic cheilitis but of unknown aetiology [2]; it presents with more persistent, heavier crusting than simple dry lips and does not resolve with lip salve alone.
problems.treatment:
- **Lip salves** applied regularly — lanolin or petroleum jelly-based emollients restore the surface barrier [1]. The patient needs to understand why: salves replace the moisture barrier that licking destroys.
- Break the licking habit. Explain the cycle — the licking is the problem, not the solution.
- Protect against wind and sunlight with a lip balm containing SPF.
- If a contact allergen is suspected, identify and remove it (toothpaste flavouring, lipstick, nickel in instruments).
- Exfoliative cheilitis of unknown aetiology: manage symptomatically, consider topical steroids if inflamed, and refer if persistent.
problems.prognosis:
- With barrier treatment and habit interruption, simple dry lips resolve completely.
- Without habit change, the cycle continues indefinitely.
- Exfoliative cheilitis and actinic cheilitis carry a worse prognosis: actinic cheilitis is premalignant and requires follow-up [3]; exfoliative cheilitis is persistent and of unknown aetiology [2].

citations.quote: Except when accompanied by frank cheilitis, this is usually entirely innocent and can be treated symptomatically. Common causes are lip licking, and exposure to wind or sunlight. It is also a manifestation of viral illness. Rx: lip salves.
This is similar to actinic cheilitis but of unknown aetiology.
Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and ↑ mitotic activity in the basal layer. Premalignant. Advise sun blocks and regular follow-up.

problems.description: Firm, diffuse swelling of the lips that comes and goes but never fully resolves. No urticaria, no anaphylaxis. Younger patient, often with oral soreness or ulcers alongside.
problems.etiology:
A granulomatous inflammation of the lips, cheeks, or face — histologically identical to Crohn's disease, showing non-caseating granuloma on biopsy [1]. It may be:

- The initial or isolated manifestation of Crohn's disease.
- Related to sarcoidosis.
- A hypersensitivity response to benzoates (found in toothpaste) or other food additives such as tomatoes [1, 2].

The condition typically develops before the third decade of life [3]. The precise mechanism is unclear, but the granulomatous response suggests a dysregulated immune reaction — probably to a food or environmental antigen in genetically susceptible individuals [2].
problems.presentation:
What you'll typically see:

- **Diffuse lip swelling** that develops slowly, fluctuates, and persists — lasting days to weeks per episode, with incomplete resolution over time [3].
- The lips progressively firm up with repeated episodes, eventually becoming persistently swollen [3].
- Perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy, or cracked; angular cheilitis can develop [3].
- Oral soreness, mouth ulcers, and a cobblestone buccal mucosa are common accompanying features [3, 4].
- No urticaria, no systemic allergy features, no rapid-onset anaphylaxis — this distinguishes it from angioedema.
problems.results:
- **Biopsy of the lip or buccal mucosa**: the defining result. Non-caseating granuloma on histology is required to confirm the diagnosis [1].
- **Patch testing for allergens**: benzoates and other food additives [1].
- **Exclusion of systemic disease**: Crohn's and sarcoidosis must be ruled out before diagnosing isolated orofacial granulomatosis [2]. Investigations include CXR, serum ACE, calcium, and gastroenterology referral if bowel symptoms are present.
- The lip swelling of OFG is expected to last days to weeks before resolving; acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve within 48 hours [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The useful contrasts:

- **Angioedema** (allergic or hereditary): rapid onset, resolves within 24–48 hours, may be triggered by a specific allergen or medication [5]. OFG is slower and more persistent.
- **Angular cheilitis**: confined to the commissures and infective in nature — OFG causes diffuse lip swelling and angular cheilitis can develop on top of it [3].
- **Crohn's disease**: OFG is histologically identical — the diagnosis of isolated OFG requires exclusion of systemic Crohn's [2].
- The cobblestone buccal mucosa and oral ulcers alongside the lip swelling are a helpful ensemble pointing to OFG rather than a purely labial condition.
problems.treatment:
Specific to the local problem:

- **Intralesional triamcinolone** injected into the affected lip — the first-line local treatment [1, 2]. 1 mL (40 mg) per injection under LA [6].
- Identify and avoid dietary allergens, particularly benzoates and tomatoes. Elimination diet guided by patch test results [1, 2].
- **Anti-TNF therapies** or **clofazimine 100–200 mg daily for 3–6 months** for refractory cases [1].
- Patients with generalised Crohn's or very severe OFG may benefit from systemic sulfasalazine or infliximab [2].
- Psychological support: lip swelling is disfiguring; ask about social impact and mood [7].
problems.prognosis:
- The progression of OFG is unpredictable; patients need to be informed of this explicitly [7].
- Allergen avoidance combined with intralesional steroid can achieve significant improvement in many cases.
- In some patients, the lip swelling becomes permanently firm and disfiguring despite treatment.
- Systemic Crohn's, if present, follows its own course independently of the oral manifestations.

citations.quote: (Orofacial granulomatosis.) This is characterized by diffuse swelling of the lips, cheeks, or face and is histologically similar to Crohn's disease (non-caseating granuloma being found on biopsy). It may be the initial manifestation of Crohn's disease or related to sarcoidosis or completely isolated. It may be an allergic reaction to benzoates (toothpaste ingredient) or tomatoes. A patch test for allergens may be indicated. Intralesional steroids, e.g. triamcinolone into affected lip, anti-TNF therapies, or clofazimine 100–200mg daily for 3–6 months may help.

This is clinically and histologically identical to oral manifestations of Crohn's disease. ∆ of exclusion (Crohn's, sarcoid). Probable aetiology is as a hypersensitivity response to certain foods, additives such as benzoates, etc. ∆ is biopsy to demonstrate granulomata histologically and exclusion of systemic disease. Rx: specific to the local problem; e.g. lips (granulomatous cheilitis) intralesional steroid. Most beneficial Rx is to identify and avoid the irritant factors. Patients who have generalized Crohn's or very severe orofacial granulomatosis may benefit from systemic Rx with sulfasalazine or infliximab.

Given the patient's age, history and clinical findings, the most likely diagnosis is orofacial granulomatosis (OFG). This condition typically develops before the third decade of life and is thought to affect both genders equally. Lip swelling affects the majority of patients, with each episode lasting days to weeks. Over time, the lips may become firm and persistently swollen. The perioral skin may become red, dry, itchy or cracked, with some patients developing angular cheilitis.
The patient reports intermittent lip swelling and a sore mouth for the last 6 months.
The lip swelling of OFG would be expected to last days to weeks before resolving. Acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve in 48 hours.
1mL (40mg) injected into lesion. Needs LA. Used in granulomatous cheilitis, intractable lichen planus, keloid scars, and painful postsurgical trigger spots.

All patients need to be informed about the nature of the disease and that its progression is unpredictable. Lip swelling is disfiguring, and it is important to ask the patient about social interactions and his mood in case psychological support is needed.

problems.description: Soft bluish or reddish lump on the lip present since birth or early childhood — blanches completely when you press on it.
problems.etiology: A developmental lesion of blood vessels — not a tumour in the conventional sense, but an abnormal proliferation of vascular tissue arising during development [1]. The reason it blanches on pressure is that it's blood-filled: pressing empties the vessels and the colour disappears, which is the clinical test that distinguishes it from a pigmented naevus or melanoma.
problems.presentation: Present at birth or appears in early childhood [1]. What you'll see is a soft, compressible swelling — bluish, reddish, or purple — on the lip or oral mucosa. It blanches completely on diascopy (pressing with a glass slide or fingertip). It can grow with the child, remain static, or spontaneously regress [1]. No pain, no ulceration in the straightforward case.
problems.results: The blanch test is the key finding — complete blanching on pressure distinguishes a haemangioma from a pigmented or solid lesion [1]. The interesting bit: **do not biopsy**, as this risks significant haemorrhage from an uncontrolled vascular lesion [1]. Diagnosis is clinical; imaging is used for deeper or large lesions.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The blanch test is pathognomonic in context — a lip swelling that completely blanches under pressure is vascular [1]. The developmental timing (present at birth or early childhood) and the capacity for spontaneous regression in 80% of cases [1] separate haemangioma from acquired vascular tumours.
problems.treatment: The rule of thumb here: watch and wait first. 80% spontaneously regress and need no intervention [1]. For the 20% that persist or grow, options include laser, cryotherapy, or excision if the lesion is very small [1]. Do not biopsy as a diagnostic step — the blanch test and clinical picture should be enough, and biopsy risks bleeding [1].
problems.prognosis: 80% of haemangiomas spontaneously regress — so the majority of cases need observation only [1]. Those that do not regress can be successfully treated with laser or cryotherapy.

citations.quote: This is a developmental lesion of blood vessels. Present at birth, they can grow with the child, remain static, or regress. Blanch on pressure. Do not biopsy. 80% spontaneously regress; Rx for those that don't: laser or cryotherapy, can be excised if very small.

problems.description: Sudden dramatic swelling of the lip, floor of mouth, or neck appearing over minutes to hours. Patient is distressed. Possible trigger (food, drug, insect sting).
problems.etiology: A severe type I allergic response affecting the lips, neck, and floor of mouth [1]. There is usually an identifiable cause [1]. The airway is the critical concern: if the floor of mouth or neck is involved, oedema can compromise the airway rapidly [2].
problems.presentation: Rapid onset swelling — lips, floor of mouth, neck — often within minutes of exposure to the trigger [1, 2]. What you'll also see in a full allergic reaction is urticaria, flushing, and in severe cases bronchospasm and cardiovascular collapse [2]. The swelling can be alarming in extent. The patient or family member may be able to name the trigger.
problems.results: This is a clinical diagnosis made on the presentation. The key question is severity: mild lip swelling alone versus swelling that involves the floor of mouth, neck, or airway [1, 2]. Angio-oedema is sudden onset, with severe face and neck allergic swelling — the airway is at risk [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing that distinguishes allergic angio-oedema from OFG: there is usually an identifiable cause [1], and it resolves within 48 hours — OFG lip swelling lasts days to weeks [3].
problems.treatment: Mild: oral antihistamine [1]. Severe — treat as anaphylaxis [1, 2]. Here's the sequence for severe cases: adrenaline (epinephrine) IM, antihistamine IV, hydrocortisone IV, oxygen, call emergency services. Airway protection is the priority — if floor of mouth and neck are involved, this is an emergency.
problems.prognosis: With prompt treatment, angio-oedema resolves. The danger is the window before treatment when airway compromise is possible [2]. Identifying and avoiding the trigger prevents recurrence.

citations.quote: Severe type I allergic response affecting lips, neck, and floor of mouth. Usually an identifiable cause. Rx: mild—antihistamine PO; severe—as anaphylaxis, …… Anaphylactic shock and other drug reactions, p. 564.
Angio-oedema is sudden onset, with severe face and neck allergic swelling. The airway is at risk and therefore should be managed as for anaphylaxis.
The lip swelling of OFG would be expected to last days to weeks before resolving. Acute inflammatory causes such as angioedema resolve in 48 hours.

problems.description: Recurrent lip, floor of mouth, or neck swelling with no clear allergen — and a family history of the same. Feet and buttocks may also swell.
problems.etiology: A defect of C1-esterase inhibitor [1]. Swelling is precipitated by trauma [1]. Family history is the key pointer.
problems.presentation: Recurrent swelling of the lips, neck, and floor of mouth — and characteristically also the feet and buttocks [1]. No urticaria, no identifiable allergen. The patient may report a positive family history. Attacks can occur after trauma, including dental treatment.
problems.results: The diagnostic workup centres on blood tests: low C4, normal C3, and absence of C1 esterase inhibitor activity [1]. Family history supports the diagnosis. This pattern separates it from allergic angio-oedema, where C4 is normal, and from OFG, where complement levels are normal and swelling is chronic.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The family history, the recurrent pattern, and the swelling at multiple sites including feet and buttocks are the key pointers [1]. Low C4, normal C3, and absence of C1 esterase inhibitor activity is the biochemical fingerprint [1].
problems.treatment: Acute attacks: fresh frozen plasma (which contains C1-esterase inhibitor) or partially purified C1-esterase inhibitor concentrate — seek advice in your locality [1]. Prophylaxis: long-term, tranexamic acid; short-term (e.g. before dental treatment), danazol [1]. Dental treatment is a known trigger — plan accordingly.
problems.prognosis: Recurrent without prophylaxis. With appropriate prophylaxis and acute management, attacks can be controlled [1]. The key risk is airway compromise during a severe episode.

citations.quote: Defect of C1-esterase inhibitor. Lip, neck, floor of mouth swelling, and swelling of feet and buttocks. Precipitated by trauma. Diagnosis from family history, bloods: low C4, normal C3, and absence of C1 esterase inhibitor activity. Rx: acute attacks—fresh frozen plasma (contains C1-esterase inhibitor) or partially purified (seek advice in your locality). Prophylaxis: long term, tranexamic acid; short term, danazol.

problems.description: Dry, thickened, keratotic lower lip with a blurred or irregular vermilion border. Long history of sun exposure. No ulceration yet but the change is progressive.
problems.etiology: Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and increased mitotic activity in the basal layer [1]. The reason the lower lip is almost exclusively affected is its direct sun-facing position — the upper lip is shaded by the philtrum. The relevance is not cosmetic: actinic cheilitis is premalignant, and its recognised relationship to lip SCC makes it a condition that needs surveillance rather than reassurance [1].
problems.presentation: What you'll see on the lower lip: drying, scaling, keratotic thickening, and blurring of the vermilion border — the sharp line between the vermilion and skin is lost [1]. The lip may appear pale or greyish rather than the normal red. The patient is typically an outdoor worker or farmer with a long history of UV exposure. No ulceration in the early phase, but any non-healing area or indurated patch raises the concern that premalignancy has tipped into SCC.
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical, but biopsy is indicated when the appearance changes, an ulcer develops, or induration appears — to exclude early SCC. Histology of actinic cheilitis shows the keratotic changes and basal-layer mitotic activity that mark it as premalignant [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key framing: this is not just dry lips. Cheilitis simplex is habit-driven and reversible with lip salve; actinic cheilitis is UV-driven, shows structural change (keratosis, vermilion border blurring), and is premalignant [1]. The difference matters because actinic cheilitis requires follow-up and sun protection, not just emollients.
problems.treatment: Advise sun blocks and arrange regular follow-up [1]. The goal is to halt further UV damage. Sun block on the lower lip at every outdoor exposure. If induration, ulceration, or rapid change develops, urgent biopsy and referral. Laser excision or vermilionectomy for active intervention when indicated.
problems.prognosis: Premalignant — the risk of progression to SCC is the main concern [1]. Regular follow-up allows early detection of any malignant transformation. Sun avoidance and sun block reduce further progression.

citations.quote: Sun damage to the lower lip causes excessive keratin production and ↑ mitotic activity in the basal layer. Premalignant. Advise sun blocks and regular follow-up.

problems.description: Disc-like white plaques on the lips or oral mucosa, recurring and persisting. Mostly women. May have a faint butterfly rash on the face.
problems.etiology: A chronic disorder where lesions are limited to skin and mucosa [1]. It can be distinguished from SLE by testing for specific double-stranded DNA antinuclear antibody in serum [1]. DLE is more likely to remain as a chronic and recurring disorder than to progress to SLE, although progression can occur [1].
problems.presentation: Disc-like white plaques on the oral mucosa and lips [1]. Oral lesions are present in 30% of cases [1]. The lip lesions in women may be premalignant — so this is a condition that needs more than just topical treatment [1]. A butterfly rash on the face may be present [1]. Patients often have a history of sun sensitivity.
problems.results: The discriminating blood test: DLE can be distinguished from SLE by the presence of specific double-stranded DNA antinuclear antibody in serum [1]. In DLE this antibody is absent; in SLE it is present. Biopsy of the oral lesion shows characteristic interface mucositis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing is, DLE and SLE share clinical features but differ in scope and serology. DLE lesions are confined to skin and mucosa [1]; SLE involves joints, kidneys, blood, and other organ systems [1]. The white plaques of DLE can resemble lichen planus — the distinction rests on serology and biopsy. In women, lip lesions are specifically flagged as potentially premalignant [1].
problems.treatment: DLE: topical steroids as first-line [1]. Refractory lesions may respond to dapsone or thalidomide [1]. For SLE: systemic steroids [1]. Refer to dermatology or oral medicine for ongoing management. Regular review of the lip lesions in women is needed given the premalignant risk [1].
problems.prognosis: DLE is more likely to remain a chronic, recurring disorder than to progress to SLE [1]. Oral lesions require long-term follow-up. Lip lesions in women carry a premalignant designation [1].

citations.quote: The lesions of this condition are limited to skin and mucosa. May present as disc-like white plaques in the mouth and can progress to SLE, although is more likely to remain as a chronic and recurring disorder. Oral lesions are present in 30%. Lip lesions in women may be premalignant. Butterfly rash may be present. DLE can be distinguished from SLE by the presence of specific double-stranded DNA antinuclear antibody in serum. Rx: SLE—systemic steroids; DLE—topical steroids, refractory lesions may respond to dapsone or thalidomide.

problems.description: Persistent vertical crack running down the middle of the lower lip. Not at the commissures. Difficult to eradicate.
problems.conditionName: Persistent median fissure of the lip
problems.etiology: May be found as a developmental abnormality, but the interesting bit is that it is usually secondarily infected, which makes it extremely difficult to eradicate [1]. May be associated with granulomatous cheilitis [1] — so when a median fissure keeps recurring despite treatment, orofacial granulomatosis should be considered.
problems.presentation: A chronic, deep midline vertical fissure on the lower lip vermilion, distinct from the commissure angular cheilitis. The patient may have had it for years. The fissure bleeds intermittently, cracks on yawning, and is resistant to simple emollient treatment [1].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis. If persistent or associated with lip swelling, consider biopsy to exclude granulomatous change. If the fissure is at the midline and recurs despite standard treatment, look for granulomatous cheilitis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Site is the distinguishing feature: the midline of the lower lip, not the commissures [1]. Angular cheilitis affects the corners; median fissure is strictly central. The association with granulomatous cheilitis is the clinical flag to look for — if lip swelling accompanies the fissure, OFG is in the differential [1].
problems.treatment: Excision plus or minus intralesional steroid [1]. The secondary infection makes simple topical treatment insufficient. If granulomatous cheilitis is associated, manage accordingly with intralesional triamcinolone.
problems.prognosis: Difficult to eradicate due to secondary infection [1]. Excision offers the best chance of resolution. Association with granulomatous cheilitis means prognosis is tied to control of the underlying condition.

citations.quote: This may be found as a developmental abnormality but is usually secondarily infected, which is extremely difficult to eradicate. May be associated with granulomatous cheilitis. Rx: excision ± intralesional steroid.

problems.description: Painful, crusted, bleeding erosions of the lips and gingiva in a young adult, often with target lesions on the palms. Preceded by a cold sore or a new drug.
problems.etiology: An immunologically mediated hypersensitivity reaction affecting skin and mucous membranes [1]. Trigger agents can be identified in about half of cases and include drugs (carbamazepine, penicillins, NSAIDs), infection (HSV, mycoplasma pneumonia), pregnancy, malignancy, sunlight, and chemicals such as perfumes and food additives [1]. Recurrent HSV infection is a particularly recognised trigger — a cold sore 1–2 weeks before lip crusting raises this possibility [2].
problems.presentation: What you'll see is oral mucosa covered in bullae that break down, with the lips and gingivae becoming crusted with painful erosions [1]. Target lesions — concentric rings of erythema — on the palms, legs, face, or neck are present in the skin form [1]. Oral lesions are seen in 70% [1]. Usually a fever is present [1]. The symptoms range from mild to life-threatening: Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis represent the severest forms of the spectrum [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is from clinical features [1]. The target lesions are characteristic. Biopsy may be needed to exclude other blistering conditions. Virological studies to exclude herpes — because if HSV is the trigger, aciclovir is part of the management [3]. The Stevens–Johnson end of the spectrum is associated with fever and multiple mucosal involvement [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of painful oral erosions with crusted lips in a young adult, plus the target-lesion skin rash, is the defining picture [1]. The thing is, the lip crusting in EM can look alarming — thick haemorrhagic crusts across the vermilion are characteristic and distinct from the gold crust of angular cheilitis or the clear crusting of herpes labialis. The trigger history (recent herpes labialis or new drug) is always worth establishing [1, 2].
problems.treatment: The goal is to withdraw or treat the trigger factor if identified [3]. Hospitalisation may be required in severe forms for supportive therapy with IV rehydration [3]. Biopsy and virological studies to exclude herpes; aciclovir may be needed if the condition is related to herpes [3]. Improve oral hygiene with 0.2% chlorhexidine mouthwash [3]. Severe form: steroids and azathioprine [3]. Minor form: topical steroids [3].
problems.prognosis: It is a self-limiting condition in 3–4 weeks [1], but can recur once or twice a year [1]. Stevens–Johnson syndrome carries a higher morbidity — hospitalisation, fluid management, and systemic treatment are required [4]. Avoiding the trigger reduces recurrence.

citations.quote: This is an immunologically mediated hypersensitivity reaction affecting skin and mucous membrane, usually in young adult males. Trigger agents can be identified in half of the cases and these include drugs (carbamazepine, penicillins, NSAIDs), infection (HSV, mycoplasma pneumonia), pregnancy, malignancy, sunlight, and chemicals such as perfumes and food additives. ∆: from clinical features which include 'target lesions', concentric rings of erythema on the palms, legs, face, or neck. Oral lesions seen in 70% in which the oral mucosa is covered in bullae which break down, the lips and gingivae becoming crusted with painful erosions. There is usually a fever. It is a self-limiting condition in 3–4 weeks but can recur once or twice a year. The symptoms range from mild to life-threatening conditions. Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) represent the severest forms of the spectrum.

If the patient has had recurrent HSV infection, usually in the form of herpes labialis, then the present ulcers could not have been caused by a primary herpetic infection. Recurrent herpetic infection is sometimes a trigger for attacks of erythema multiforme and a cold sore 1–2 weeks before onset would raise this possibility.

Withdraw or treat trigger factor if identified. Hospitalization may be required in severe forms for supportive therapy with IV rehydration. Biopsy; virological studies to exclude herpes; aciclovir may be needed if it is related to herpes. Improve OH with 0.2% chlorhexidine mouthwash. Severe form: Rx with steroids and azathioprine. Minor form: Rx with topical steroids.

A severe version of erythema multiforme, a mucocutaneous condition that is probably autoimmune in nature and precipitated particularly by drugs. Classical signs are the target lesions, concentric red rings which especially affect the hands and feet. Stevens–Johnson syndrome is said to be present when the condition is particularly severe, and is associated with fever and multiple mucosal involvement. Viral infections, e.g. herpes simplex, are the second commonest cause.

problems.description: Flat, dark brown or black spots scattered around the mouth and on the inner cheeks in a young person. Family history. Possibly some gut symptoms.
problems.etiology: An autosomal dominant condition combining melanotic pigmentation of the perioral skin and mucosa with intestinal polyposis [1]. The polyps are hamartomatous — not true adenomas — and are found in the small intestine [1]. The reason this matters clinically is that although the polyps themselves have no particular propensity to malignant change, they can cause intussusception or other forms of gut obstruction [1].
problems.presentation: Flat, dark pigmented macules — melanotic spots — on the perioral skin (especially around the mouth) and on the oral mucosa [1]. Present from childhood, autosomal dominant so family members may be affected. There may be associated gut symptoms: abdominal pain or obstruction from intussusception [1]. Ovarian tumours are sometimes associated (10% of women with the syndrome) [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is clinical when perioral pigmentation is combined with the family history and gut polyposis. The thing is, if you spot the perioral melanosis, the gut needs investigating — hamartomatous small intestinal polyps and their obstructive potential are the systemic concern [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Multiple small dark macules clustered around the mouth in a young person with a family history is a pattern that should prompt gastrointestinal investigation [1]. The gut polyps are hamartomatous and carry a risk of intussusception rather than malignant transformation [1].
problems.treatment: Refer to gastroenterology for GI surveillance — the gut polyps can obstruct [1]. Genetic counselling given the autosomal dominant inheritance [1]. The perioral lesions themselves are benign and do not require treatment. Monitor for associated ovarian tumours in women [1].
problems.prognosis: The perioral lesions are benign. The intestinal polyps carry a risk of intussusception and gut obstruction but not of malignant transformation [1]. The 10% ovarian tumour association in women warrants monitoring [1].

citations.quote: An autosomal dominant condition of melanotic pigmentation of skin (especially peri-oral skin) and mucosa, and intestinal polyposis. These polyps, unlike those of Gardener syndrome, have no particular propensity to malignant change, being hamartomatous, and are found in the small intestine. They may, however, cause intussusception or other forms of gut obstruction. Ovarian tumours are sometimes associated with the condition (10% of woman with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome).

problems.description: Middle-aged woman with angular cheilitis, difficulty swallowing, and spooned nails. Looks pale and tired.
problems.etiology: The occurrence of dysphagia, microcytic hypochromic anaemia, koilonychia, and angular cheilitis [1]. The mechanism connecting these signs is iron deficiency — the koilonychia and angular cheilitis are secondary to the anaemia, though they may be the presenting features that bring the patient to the dental chair [1]. The dysphagia arises from a post-cricoid web, a membrane on the anterior oesophageal wall, which is itself premalignant [1].
problems.presentation: What you'll see in the dental chair: angular cheilitis and a pale patient who struggles to swallow [1]. The history reveals difficulty swallowing solids, fatigue, and pallor. Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails) and angular cheilitis together in a middle-aged woman are the classic ensemble [1]. The main affected group is middle-aged women [1].
problems.results: Blood tests will show microcytic hypochromic anaemia [1]. The oesophageal web is found on barium swallow or endoscopy. The reason this matters beyond the angular cheilitis is the premalignant post-cricoid web — correction of the anaemia may both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The interesting bit is that the dental features (angular cheilitis) are not the main clinical problem — they are the secondary manifestation of a systemic iron-deficiency anaemia with a serious oesophageal complication [1]. What distinguishes this from simple angular cheilitis is the systemic picture: dysphagia, anaemia, and koilonychia together make a syndrome, not just a soft-tissue finding at the commissures.
problems.treatment: Correct the anaemia — correction of anaemia may both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression of the oesophageal web [1]. Refer to gastroenterology for assessment of the oesophageal web.
problems.prognosis: Correction of anaemia can both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression of the post-cricoid web [1]. The premalignant nature of the web means that failure to diagnose and treat carries a risk of post-cricoid carcinoma.

citations.quote: The occurrence of dysphagia, microcytic hypochromic anaemia, koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), and angular cheilitis. The dysphagia is due to a post-cricoid web, usually a membrane on the anterior oesophageal wall, which is premalignant. The koilonychia and angular cheilitis are 2° to the anaemia but may be presenting symptoms. The main affected group is middle-aged women, and correction of the anaemia may both relieve symptoms and prevent malignant progression of the web.

problems.description: Young child under five with cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, red eyes, and a fever. Cervical lymph nodes enlarged.
problems.etiology: A systemic vasculitis affecting children under 5 years old [1]. The aetiology is not fully characterised in the source. Arteritis is the most serious complication, and without treatment the condition can be fatal — though with treatment the death rate in the UK is less than 4% [2].
problems.presentation: The diagnostic criteria include: red, dry cracked lips; strawberry tongue; erythematous oropharyngeal mucosa; bilateral conjunctivitis; cervical lymphadenopathy; generalised rash; desquamation of hands and feet; and fever [2]. What happens is that the oral features — the cracked lips and strawberry tongue — can be the first things a dentist notices. If suspected, immediate paediatric referral is mandatory [2].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis based on the criteria above [2]. No single laboratory test confirms the diagnosis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The ensemble of cracked lips, strawberry tongue, bilateral conjunctivitis, lymphadenopathy, rash, and fever in a child under 5 is diagnostic [2]. The thing is, no single feature is specific — it's the combination across sites and systems that makes the diagnosis. From the dental chair, cracked red lips and a strawberry tongue in an unwell febrile child should trigger immediate concern.
problems.treatment: If suspected, refer to a paediatrician immediately [2]. Hospital treatment with immunoglobulin and aspirin is the mainstay [1]. Speed matters — early treatment reduces the risk of coronary artery complications.
problems.prognosis: Can be treated if diagnosed [2]. Death rate in the UK is less than 4% with treatment, and approximately 0.1% in the US and Japan [2].

citations.quote: Usually affects children <5yrs with pyrexia, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, dry cracked lips, red eyes, and red fingers and toes. Arteritis is the most serious complication. Immunoglobulin and aspirin in hospital is the mainstay of Rx.

This systemic vasculitis affecting children <5yrs causes death in the UK in <4% (US and Japan ~0.1%).4 It can be treated if ∆. The criteria include red, dry cracked lips, strawberry tongue, and erythematous oropharyngeal mucosa, bilateral conjunctivitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, generalized rash, desquamation of hands and feet, and fever. If suspected, refer to a paediatrician.

problems.description: Bilateral parotid and lacrimal gland swelling with eye inflammation in a young adult. Possible facial nerve palsy.
problems.etiology: A variant of sarcoidosis — the same granulomatous condition, but with a specific combination of lacrimal and salivary (especially parotid) swelling, uveitis, and fever [1]. Sometimes there are associated neuropathies, such as facial palsy [1]. The reason it's worth knowing in a dental context is that the parotid swelling brings these patients into dental and maxillofacial awareness.
problems.presentation: Bilateral parotid enlargement, lacrimal gland swelling, uveitis (eye inflammation), and fever [1]. Facial nerve palsy may be present alongside [1]. The patient may present primarily with parotid swelling, which can look like other salivary disease. The combination with uveitis and fever is the distinguishing picture.
problems.results: CXR shows hilar lymphadenopathy (sarcoidosis). Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme and calcium are raised. Biopsy of accessible tissue reveals non-caseating granuloma. Ophthalmology review is needed for uveitis.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of parotid swelling, lacrimal swelling, uveitis, and fever in the context of sarcoidosis is the defining picture [1]. So parotid swelling in a young adult is not always a salivary stone or tumour — if there is eye involvement and systemic features, Heerfordt syndrome belongs on the differential.
problems.treatment: This is sarcoidosis — systemic steroids are the main treatment, intralesional or systemic [2]. Ophthalmology referral for the uveitis is mandatory. Refer to respiratory or general medicine for the systemic sarcoidosis workup.
problems.prognosis: Sarcoidosis can be self-limiting or chronic. Mortality rate for disseminated systemic disease is 10–20% [2].

citations.quote: Sarcoidosis with associated lacrimal and salivary (especially parotid) swelling, uveitis, and fever. Sometimes there are associated neuropathies, e.g. facial palsy.

A chronic multisystem granulomatous condition of young adults (more common in black people). Lip swelling, and gingival and palatal nodules occur. Heerfordt syndrome, …… Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever), p. 784. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granuloma with inclusion bodies in 20–50%). CXR: hilar lymphadenopathy. Serum adenosine deaminase, angiotensin-converting enzyme, and calcium level is i. Ask an ophthalmologist to exclude uveal tract involvement. Mortality rate for disseminated systemic disease is 10–20%. Rx: steroids, intralesional or systemic.

problems.description: Multiple small lumpy nodules on the lips and tongue in a tall, thin young person. Possibly a thyroid lump or raised blood pressure.
problems.conditionName: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type IIb (MEN IIb)
problems.etiology: A group of conditions affecting the endocrine glands. MEN IIb consists of multiple mucosal neuromas with a characteristic histopathology, phaeochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and a thin wasted appearance [1]. The oral neuromas appear as multiple lumps on the lips and tongue. Calcitonin levels are elevated if medullary thyroid carcinoma is present [1].
problems.presentation: Multiple mucosal neuromas on the lips and tongue in a tall, thin, wasted-looking child or young adult [1]. The thin, wasted appearance is part of the syndrome phenotype. The patient may also have features of phaeochromocytoma (hypertension, sweating) or medullary thyroid carcinoma (thyroid lump) — though the oral neuromas may be the presenting feature [1].
problems.results: Biopsy of an oral nodule is mandatory — histopathology will show characteristic neuroma [1]. If histopathology is suggestive, the thyroid must be adequately investigated [1]. Calcitonin level should be measured [1]. Raised calcitonin confirms medullary thyroid carcinoma. Urine catecholamines for phaeochromocytoma.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The rule of thumb: multiple mucosal lumps on the lips and tongue in a tall thin young person is a 'worthwhile' syndrome — the source explicitly flags this as a diagnosis not to miss because of the associated medullary thyroid carcinoma [1]. Index of suspicion should be high [1]. The combination of oral neuromas, phaeochromocytoma, and medullary thyroid carcinoma is pathognomonic of MEN IIb.
problems.treatment: Biopsy the oral lesions [1]. If histopathology is suggestive, investigate the thyroid adequately [1]. Refer to endocrinology for full workup and management of the thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma. Medullary thyroid carcinoma requires surgery.
problems.prognosis: This is another 'worthwhile' syndrome — a source designation meaning the diagnosis is worth making because early treatment of the associated malignancies can be life-saving [1]. Prognosis depends primarily on the medullary thyroid carcinoma and its stage at detection.

citations.quote: A group of conditions affecting the endocrine glands. MEN IIb is of particular relevance as it consists of multiple mucosal neuromas which have a characteristic histopathology, phaeochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and a thin wasted appearance. Calcitonin levels are elevated if medullary thyroid carcinoma is present. Index of suspicion should be high in tall, thin, wasted-looking children and young adults presenting with lumps in the mouth. Biopsy is mandatory and if histopathology is suggestive the thyroid must be adequately investigated. This is another 'worthwhile' syndrome.

problems.description: Child with intellectual disability and severe repetitive self-inflicted wounds to the lips from biting.
problems.etiology: A defect of purine metabolism causing intellectual disability, spastic cerebral palsy, choreoathetosis, and aggressive self-mutilating behaviour — particularly involving the lips [1].
problems.presentation: Severe, repetitive self-inflicted trauma to the lips from biting in a child with intellectual disability and neurological features (spasticity, choreoathetosis) [1]. The lips may be extensively scarred or mutilated. The self-mutilation is a defining and distressing feature — the child cannot prevent it [1].
problems.results: Diagnosis is based on the clinical picture: intellectual disability, movement disorder (spastic cerebral palsy, choreoathetosis), and compulsive self-mutilation of the lips [1]. The condition requires paediatric neurology and metabolic medicine input.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The combination of compulsive self-mutilation of the lips and oral tissues with the neurological picture (intellectual disability, cerebral palsy, choreoathetosis) is the defining picture [1]. So in a child presenting with severe self-inflicted lip trauma, this metabolic diagnosis is in the differential — the behaviour is not simple parafunctional habit but a feature of the underlying syndrome.
problems.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary. The dental role is to protect the oral tissues from ongoing self-inflicted trauma.
problems.prognosis: The condition is lifelong. Neurological damage is permanent [1]. The goal is to manage the self-mutilating behaviour and protect the oral and perioral tissues from further damage.

citations.quote: A defect of purine metabolism causing intellectual disability, spastic cerebral palsy, choreoathetosis, and aggressive self-mutilating behaviour (particularly involving the lips).

problems.description: Small pits or sinuses on the lower lip — like tiny holes — alongside or instead of a cleft lip or palate.
problems.etiology: Present in 1–2% of cleft patients [1]. Lip pits are actually small sinuses connecting to minor salivary glands — not simple dimples [1]. The condition is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance [1].
problems.presentation: Small, symmetric pits or sinuses on the vermilion of the lower lip, usually bilateral and paramedian [1]. Typically associated with cleft lip and/or palate, though the lip pits may appear without overt clefting [1]. Second premolars are missing in 10–20% of cases [1].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis: the combination of lip pits and cleft lip/palate in a child with an autosomal dominant family history is diagnostic [1]. Check for missing second premolars on panoramic radiography [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key feature is the pits themselves — small sinuses to minor salivary glands on the lower lip vermilion [1]. This is not angular cheilitis, not mucocele, not a normal anatomical variant. The association with cleft lip/palate and missing second premolars in an autosomal dominant pattern completes the picture [1].
problems.treatment: Manage the cleft lip and palate in the usual multidisciplinary way. The lip pits themselves can be excised if symptomatic. Plan for possible missing second premolars in the restorative planning [1].
problems.prognosis: The lip pits and cleft are structural — correctable with surgery. The dental hypodontia (missing second premolars in 10–20%) requires long-term prosthetic or orthodontic planning [1].

citations.quote: Present in 1–2% of cleft patients, lip pits (which are actually small sinuses to minor salivary glands) associated with cleft lip &/or palate. Autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. Second premolars are missing in 10–20%.

problems.description: Cleft lip and/or palate in a child with missing teeth, extra teeth, and abnormalities of the fingers.
problems.etiology: One of the many cleft lip and palate syndromes, all of which are associated with hypodontia (particularly missing lateral incisors) and supernumeraries [1]. This particular one has finger abnormalities as well [1]. The combination of orofacial clefting with digital anomalies places it in the orofacial-digital group.
problems.presentation: Cleft lip and/or palate combined with hypodontia of lateral incisors, supernumerary teeth, and finger abnormalities [1]. Dental development is complex — missing teeth and extra teeth both need to be identified on imaging.
problems.results: Panoramic radiograph to assess the full dental pattern — hypodontia of laterals and supernumeraries [1]. Multidisciplinary assessment for the cleft and the digital anomalies. Genetic evaluation for classification within the orofacial-digital group.
problems.definingCharacteristics: What makes this entry worth flagging: a cleft lip/palate child with both hypodontia and supernumerary teeth and finger abnormalities is not a straightforward isolated cleft — the digital element points to a syndromic diagnosis [1].
problems.treatment: Multidisciplinary cleft team management for the lip and palate. Orthodontic and restorative planning for the complex dental pattern — missing laterals and supernumeraries require a coordinated treatment plan [1].
problems.prognosis: Dental rehabilitation is complex given the combination of hypodontia and supernumeraries [1]. Overall prognosis is guided by the severity of the digital anomalies and the success of the cleft repair.

citations.quote: One of the many CLP syndromes, all of which are associated with hypodontia (laterals especially) and supernumeraries. This one has finger abnormalities as well.

problems.description: Patches of pale, depigmented skin around the mouth or on the lips. May also involve the oral mucosa.
problems.etiology: Vitiligo is a depigmentation condition that can involve perioral skin and occasionally oral mucosa [1].
problems.presentation: Patches of depigmented skin around the mouth or on the lip. The patient may present incidentally during a dental examination.
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic depigmented patches in their perioral distribution.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Perioral depigmentation with no associated ulceration or keratosis — the patient may present incidentally. The condition is listed among those affecting the lip [1].
problems.treatment: The perioral skin is in the domain of dermatology.
problems.prognosis: Vitiligo is generally a chronic condition.

problems.description: Persistent, recurring scaling and crusting of the vermilion lip border. No known cause. Resists simple emollient treatment.
problems.etiology: This is similar to actinic cheilitis but of unknown aetiology [1]. The reason simple emollient treatment fails is that, unlike cheilitis simplex (which is habit-driven and reversible), exfoliative cheilitis has no identifiable driving cause to remove.
problems.presentation: Persistent scaling and crusting of the vermilion lip border that keeps recurring despite treatment [1]. The crusting is heavier and more persistent than in simple dry lips. No vesiculation, no commissure involvement. The patient may report that the lip repeatedly forms a dry crust that peels off and then re-forms.
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis based on the persistent, idiopathic nature of the crusting. Biopsy is performed if there is any doubt — to exclude actinic cheilitis (which shows keratotic basal-layer changes), lichen planus, or early malignant change. There is no definitive diagnostic test.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The thing that distinguishes exfoliative cheilitis from its close neighbours: it is similar to actinic cheilitis in appearance but lacks the UV history and basal-layer mitotic changes [1]. It is more persistent and heavier than simple dry lips (cheilitis simplex), which resolves with emollient and habit correction. The unknown aetiology is itself a defining feature — no sun exposure, no identifiable allergen, no habit that fully explains it [1].
problems.treatment: Symptomatic management — topical steroids if inflamed, emollients for barrier support. Explore anxiety and lip-licking as contributing factors. Refer to oral medicine if the condition is persistent or if the diagnosis is uncertain.
problems.prognosis: Persistent and difficult to treat — the unknown aetiology means management is suppressive rather than curative [1].
